title: Lazy Propagation, and Choosing a Range-Query Structure
oneLiner: How a segment tree handles "add x to a whole range" in O(log n) by postponing work, and a decision guide for prefix sums, difference arrays, sparse tables, Fenwick trees and segment trees.
keyTakeaway: When an update covers a node's whole range, fix that node's summary now and leave a lazy tag ("my children still owe +x") instead of visiting the children. Push the tag down only when a later operation needs to go below that node. Range update and range query both stay O(log n). Pick the simplest structure that fits: static data, prefix sums or a sparse table; point updates with sums, a Fenwick tree; anything else, a segment tree.
explanation:
The segment tree in the previous lesson handles point updates. A range update such as "add 3 to every element in [2, 6]" would be one point update per element, O(n log n) for a wide range, which is worse than editing the array directly. Lazy propagation makes a range update O(log n) as well.

The idea is to postpone work. Walk the tree as a range query would. When the update's range completely covers a node, update that node's own summary right away (for sums: add delta times the number of elements it covers) and record a lazy tag on it: a note that says "every element below me should also get +delta, but I haven't told my children yet". Don't visit the children. Partly covered nodes recurse into both children and then recompute themselves, exactly like a point update.

The tag is paid off later, only if needed. Before any operation (update or query) goes below a node that carries a tag, it pushes the tag down: apply it to both children (adjust their sums, add to their tags) and clear it on the parent. This push-down step is the propagation. A query that stops at a fully covered node never needs to push, because that node's summary is already correct. Each operation still visits O(log n) nodes, so range update plus range query costs O(log n) each.

Tags have to combine. Two adds merge into one add (+3 then +2 is +5). Mixing "assign x" with "add d" needs an order rule: an assign wipes any pending add. Getting that composition right is the hard part of harder lazy problems.

At interview level you are rarely asked to code full lazy propagation in 45 minutes, but you should be able to explain it, say when it's needed, and know the cheaper tools:

Difference array: when every update comes before every query (offline), add delta at l and -delta at r + 1, then take one prefix pass. O(n + q), no tree at all.

Range add, point query, interleaved: the same difference array inside a Fenwick tree (graded in this track as Range Add, Point Query).

Range add and range sum, interleaved: lazy segment tree, or two Fenwick trees (a known trick that keeps the sum of delta and of delta times index).

Static array, min or max: a sparse table, which stores the min of every window whose length is a power of two, O(n log n) to build, and answers [l, r] in O(1) from two overlapping windows.

Point updates with sums or counts: Fenwick tree. Point updates with min, max or another associative operation: segment tree.

Counting smaller or larger elements before or after each position: Fenwick tree over compressed values, or merge sort.

The widgets: step through range adds and queries on a lazy segment tree and watch tags appear and get pushed down, then test yourself on which structure fits each scenario.
